tbl6_1: A three-column reference table listing smoothness classes against their Fourier-coefficient decay rates and a representative example for each, ranging from bounded-variation functions decaying like one over k up to band-limited functions with compactly supported spectra; the takeaway is that greater smoothness yields progressively faster decay.
fig6_1: A semi-log plot of Fourier-coefficient magnitude versus wavenumber k for three test functions, with the vertical axis logarithmic and the horizontal axis linear. The piecewise-smooth absolute-sine-cubed function gives a slowly bending downward curve (algebraic decay like k to the power minus four), the strip-analytic one over one-plus-sine-squared traces a nearly straight descending line (geometric decay), and the entire function e to the sine of x falls off faster than any straight line (super-geometric decay), cleanly separating the three smoothness regimes.
fig6_2: A three-panel illustration of aliasing. Left: a sine plus a higher-frequency sine sampled at only twelve points, where an interpolant drawn through the samples follows a misleading low-frequency curve rather than the true rapid oscillation. Center: a frequency-folding diagram showing how wavenumbers ten and minus ten outside the resolvable band fold back into the range minus six to six. Right: a comparison of the true spectrum computed from many samples against the aliased spectrum from few samples, where unresolved high modes contaminate the low ones.
fig6_3: A semi-log convergence plot with maximum-norm spectral differentiation error on the logarithmic vertical axis versus the number of grid points N on the horizontal axis, for three functions of increasing smoothness. The only-twice-differentiable absolute-sine-cubed function declines slowly along an algebraic trend like N to the power minus three; the strip-analytic one over one-plus-sine-squared falls as a straight line indicating geometric convergence; and the entire function e to the sine of x plunges almost vertically to machine precision near N equals thirty, demonstrating super-geometric convergence as predicted by the differentiation theorem.
